directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; bracted viburnum is a rare native selected for good garden performance and drought tolerance once established. Flat clusters of small white flowers open in mid-spring on a dense, upright shrub with dark green, toothed leaves, followed by blue-black fruit that provides food for birds into fall, a garden performance similar to more commonly grown viburnums but from an uncommon Georgia native species discovered along the Savannah River in the twentieth century. Its combination of good drought tolerance, dense habit, and reliable spring bloom and fall fruit makes it a worthwhile, less common alternative to more commonly planted viburnum species for a native shrub border or wildlife garden. Water during establishment, then rely mainly on natural rainfall, and prune lightly after flowering if shaping is needed.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fragrant viburnum blooms on bare branches in late winter, so protect from hard freezes during the flowering window in colder zones.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fragrant viburnum blooms on bare branches in late winter, so protect from hard freezes during the flowering window in colder zones. Clusters of small, tubular, pale pink flowers open on bare branches in late winter to very early spring, well ahead of most other flowering shrubs, releasing an intense, sweet, clove-like fragrance that carries a surprising distance on a still winter day. Native to northern China, it is one of the earliest viburnums to bloom each year, providing welcome color and fragrance during the last weeks of winter dormancy, though an unusually hard late freeze can damage open flowers in colder parts of its range. Prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed, since it blooms on the previous year's wood, and site where its winter fragrance can be enjoyed near a door or path.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Middendorff weigela is the only yellow-flowered weigela species, distinct from the pink, red, and white tones of common hybrid weigela.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Middendorff weigela is the only yellow-flowered weigela species, distinct from the pink, red, and white tones of common hybrid weigela. Funnel-shaped flowers open a soft primrose-yellow marked with fine orange spotting in the throat, an unusual color among weigelas, which are overwhelmingly bred in shades of pink, red, and white, blooming on a compact, low-growing shrub native to cold woodland edges in northeastern Asia and Japan. Its distinctive yellow flower color and smaller stature compared to common hybrid weigela cultivars make it a worthwhile specialty addition to a shrub border or collector's garden seeking something beyond the usual pink and red weigela palette. Prune immediately after flowering to shape, since it blooms on the previous year's wood like other weigela species.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Lemoine deutzia is a classic, cold-hardy hybrid valued for its profuse, pure white late-spring flower display. This historic French hybrid, bred by the renowned Lemoine nursery in the late nineteenth century, smothers its arching branches in dense clusters of small, pure white, star-shaped flowers in late spring, one of the most floriferous of the classic deutzia hybrids and a mainstay of cottage-garden and heritage shrub borders for over a century. Reliable and easy-care, it tolerates a range of soils and climates, providing a reliable flush of white bloom each spring with minimal maintenance beyond occasional renewal pruning. Prune immediately after flowering to shape and remove some of the oldest canes at the base periodically to keep the shrub renewed and full from the ground up.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; evergreen mock orange is less cold-hardy than northern mock orange species and best suited to zones 7-9.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; evergreen mock orange is less cold-hardy than northern mock orange species and best suited to zones 7-9. Fragrant, creamy white, single flowers open along arching, semi-scrambling branches in late spring, carrying the classic sweet orange-blossom scent typical of the genus, on a Mexican native species that holds its glossy foliage semi-evergreen through mild winters in warmer zones where deciduous mock orange relatives lose their leaves. Its sprawling, somewhat vine-like habit makes it useful for training against a wall or trellis as much as a freestanding shrub, and its milder climate tolerance broadens the range of conditions where fragrant mock orange bloom can be enjoyed. Prune immediately after flowering to shape, and provide some winter protection at the colder edge of its hardiness range.
